title: Diagnostic overshadowing
blurb: Recognise when illness is being blamed on a person's learning disability or autism, and use baselines, carers and assessment to find the real cause.
question: Ben, 31, has a severe learning disability and no speech. Over two days he has stopped eating and keeps pushing staff away. A support worker writes 'challenging behaviour again' in his notes. What risk does this entry show, and what should the nurse do?

teach.body: Diagnostic overshadowing means attributing the signs or symptoms of physical or mental ill health to a person's learning disability or autism, so the real illness is missed. It appears again and again in Death by Indifference, CIPOLD, LeDeR and the death of Oliver McGowan. In plain English: 'that's just his behaviour' or 'that's his learning disability' can hide pain, infection, constipation, depression or a life-threatening illness.

teach.h: Behaviour change can mean pain or illness
head: What you see
Possible hidden cause
teach.caption: Behaviour is communication, especially for people who do not use speech.

teach.body: You cannot see a change unless you know what usual looks like. Families and long-term carers know the person's baseline: how they look, sound and behave when content and when distressed. NICE NG54 says to take account of differences in how mental health problems present and to use carers' information about behaviour change. Tools such as DisDAT turn that knowledge into a written baseline.

teach.caption: Example cues only: DisDAT records each person's own signs. It is a baseline record, not a scoring tool.

teach.body: Ben, 31, has no speech and has stopped eating and pushed staff away for two days. The nurse recognises the entry 'challenging behaviour again' as overshadowing. She compares with his DisDAT and asks staff who know him what is different: he usually loves breakfast and has been holding his jaw. She does a full set of observations, checks his bowel chart and mouth, and arranges an urgent dental and medical review. She records the change from baseline, not a label.

steps.label: Assess physically
steps.sub: Observations, pain, bowels, mouth, ears, skin

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: SBAR: say what has changed from baseline

items: Lead with the change: 'This is not his usual behaviour; his carers say he is very different.'
Give observations, including any NEWS2 score, and say that it must be read against his baseline.
State what you are worried about (for example pain, infection, bowel obstruction) and what you need.
If you are not satisfied, escalate again: carer concern is a reason to act, not to wait.

teach.text: Do not refer new or changed behaviour straight to a behaviour team, or reach for sedation, before physical and mental health causes have been looked for. A learning disability is never the explanation for a new symptom until illness has been ruled out.

items: Diagnostic overshadowing: attributing signs of illness to the learning disability or autism.
Behaviour change can be the only sign of pain or illness.
Use the baseline: families, carers, passport and DisDAT (content and distress cues).
Assess physically first; escalate with SBAR, stating the change from baseline.
Mental illness can be overshadowed too: presentations differ (NG54).

summary: You can now define diagnostic overshadowing, spot it in notes and conversations, and respond by comparing with the person's baseline, assessing physically and escalating clearly. You also know how DisDAT and carers' knowledge help.

A.q: During induction to a learning disability liaison team, Lauren is asked to define diagnostic overshadowing. Which definition is correct?
options: Missing a learning disability because a physical illness dominates
Delaying diagnosis because the person cannot consent to tests
Giving two diagnoses when one explains all the symptoms
Attributing signs of illness to the person's learning disability or autism
A.why: Diagnostic overshadowing is attributing signs or symptoms of physical or mental ill health to the learning disability or autism, so the illness is missed.

whyNot.0: This reverses the concept: the disability overshadows the illness, not the other way round.
whyNot.1: Delays over consent are a separate problem; overshadowing is about wrong attribution.

A.q: Ben, 31, has a severe learning disability and no speech. Over two days he has stopped eating and has been pushing staff away. A support worker writes 'challenging behaviour again'. Which risk does this entry show?
options: Confirmation of consent
Diagnostic overshadowing
Positive risk-taking
Restrictive practice
A.why: Labelling a change in eating and behaviour as 'challenging behaviour' attributes it to his disability and risks missing illness or pain.

whyNot.0: Consent is not the issue in this entry.
whyNot.2: Positive risk-taking is a planned approach to enabling choice, not a label for new symptoms.
whyNot.3: Nothing restrictive has been done; the risk is a missed diagnosis.

A.q: A nurse is completing a DisDAT for Ellie, 35, who has a profound learning disability. What is the main purpose of the tool?
options: To record her usual content and distress cues as a baseline
To give a numerical pain score at each observation
To diagnose the cause of her pain from her behaviour
To decide whether she has capacity to report pain
A.why: DisDAT documents the person's own content and distress cues (face, eyes, skin, sounds, habits, posture) to create a baseline. It is not a scoring tool.

whyNot.1: DisDAT is not a scoring tool.
whyNot.2: It helps recognise distress but does not diagnose its cause.
whyNot.3: It is not a capacity assessment.

B.q: Josh, 19, has a learning disability and autism. His family say he has been hitting the side of his head much more than usual for three days and is sleeping poorly. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Refer him to the behaviour support team for a new plan
Ask the GP about medication to reduce his agitation
Arrange a physical assessment for ear or dental pain
Advise the family to use planned ignoring of it
B.why: A change in self-injury focused on the head may signal ear, dental or other pain. Physical causes should be assessed before a behavioural explanation is accepted.

whyNot.0: Behaviour support may help later, but physical causes come first.
whyNot.1: Medicating the behaviour risks masking an underlying cause.
whyNot.3: Planned ignoring before assessment risks missing pain.

B.q: Sana, a staff nurse, believes that Ivy, 50, who has a learning disability, has abdominal pain: Ivy keeps rocking and holding her stomach, which her carer says is new. The doctor says, 'That is just her behaviour.' What should Sana do?
options: Accept the doctor's view and note the behaviour
Give a PRN sedative to settle Ivy until morning
Ask Ivy's carer to speak to the doctor instead
Restate the change from baseline using SBAR and escalate
B.why: The change is new according to the person who knows Ivy's baseline. Sana should restate the concern clearly with SBAR and escalate further if needed.

whyNot.0: Accepting the label risks a missed diagnosis.
whyNot.1: Sedation could mask pain and delay diagnosis.
whyNot.2: The carer's input is valuable, but the nurse remains responsible for escalating.

B.q: Leah, 28, has a moderate learning disability. Over six weeks she has stopped going to her art group, is tearful and is waking at 4 am. Day centre staff say she is 'just being moody'. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Encourage staff to motivate her back to the group
Wait to see whether her mood improves over summer
Assess for depression, allowing for a different presentation
Record it as a behaviour linked to her disability
B.why: Mental illness can be overshadowed too. NG54 1.1.2: take account of how mental health problems may present differently in people with a learning disability.

whyNot.0: Motivation alone does not address a possible depressive illness.
whyNot.1: Waiting delays assessment of a clear change.
whyNot.3: This is diagnostic overshadowing of a possible mental illness.

C.q: Ryan, 37, has a learning disability. Over a month he has started pushing his plate away and shouting at mealtimes, and he has lost 3 kg. His support team ask for a behaviour plan. What should the community nurse do first?
options: Assess for physical causes such as dental pain
Start ABC charts at mealtimes for the next six weeks
Offer smaller meals made from his favourite foods
Agree a plan to remove his plate when he shouts
C.why: Food refusal, distress at meals and weight loss point to possible dental pain, reflux or dysphagia. Physical causes must be excluded before a behavioural approach.

whyNot.1: ABC charts may help later, but six weeks' delay risks missing illness.
whyNot.2: Changing food without assessment may mask a swallowing or gut problem.
whyNot.3: This is a reactive behavioural response that ignores possible pain.

C.q: Peter, 44, has a learning disability and is on a medical ward. His NEWS2 score is 2. His long-term carer says he is very sleepy, not eating and 'nothing like himself'. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure the carer that a score of 2 is low risk
Recheck his observations at the next routine round
Ask the carer to come back when he is more awake
Reassess him now and escalate the carer's concern
C.why: NEWS2 must be read against the person's baseline, and carer concern about a change is a reason to reassess now and escalate, avoiding overshadowing.

whyNot.0: A low score does not override a significant change from baseline.
whyNot.1: Waiting for a routine round delays action on a reported deterioration.
whyNot.2: This dismisses the person who knows his baseline best.

C.q: Grace, 48, has Down syndrome. Her support staff report she has become irritable and slower over three months and want a dementia referral. What should be checked first?
options: Her IQ, to measure how much ability she has lost
Her thyroid function and other treatable causes
Her sleep pattern, to plan an earlier bedtime
Her diet, to see whether she needs supplements
C.why: Hypothyroidism is common in Down syndrome and can mimic dementia or depression, so thyroid function and other treatable causes are checked before assuming dementia.

whyNot.0: IQ testing does not identify a treatable cause.
whyNot.2: Sleep may be relevant, but treatable medical causes come first.
whyNot.3: Diet is not the first check for a change like this.

reteach.title: Change first, label never
reteach.question: What should you do the moment someone says 'that's just his learning disability'?

blocks.body: If the behaviour or symptom is new or different for this person, it needs an explanation. Ask people who know them, compare with the baseline, check the body (pain, bowels, mouth, ears, chest, skin, mood) and escalate what has changed. Only then consider a behavioural explanation.

children.label: Assess for illness and pain; escalate

blocks.text: A low early warning score does not cancel out a carer's report that the person is very different from usual.

explain.body: Diagnostic overshadowing: attributing signs or symptoms of physical or mental illness to the learning disability or autism, so the illness is missed.

test.q: Which comment from a colleague is the clearest example of diagnostic overshadowing?
options: 'Let's check his bowels as he seems uncomfortable'
'His mum says he is different today; I'll reassess'
'He always screams, it's part of his disability'
'Can we look at his passport for his pain signs?'
test.why: Attributing screaming to the disability without checking for change or cause is diagnostic overshadowing.

whyNot.0: Checking bowels is looking for a physical cause.
whyNot.1: Acting on a family's report of change is good practice.
whyNot.3: Using the passport to read pain is good practice.

explain.body: Families and carers know the person's usual self. DisDAT records content and distress cues. NG54 says to use carers' information on behaviour change.

test.q: Which source is most useful for judging whether a non-verbal person's behaviour is a change from usual?
options: A general pain score validated in adults
The person's long-term carers and their DisDAT
The ward's average length of stay data
A textbook list of learning disability traits
test.why: People who know the person well, and a DisDAT recording their own cues, show what is usual and what has changed.

whyNot.0: A general score may not fit someone who cannot self-report.
whyNot.2: Ward data says nothing about this person's baseline.
whyNot.3: Generic traits encourage overshadowing instead of individual comparison.

explain.body: Head-hitting can mean ear or dental pain; food refusal can mean dental pain, reflux or dysphagia; rocking and holding the abdomen can mean constipation; loss of skills can mean thyroid disease.

test.q: Tom, 29, has a learning disability and has been rocking and holding his abdomen for two days. What should the nurse check first?
options: His bowel chart and abdomen for constipation
His activity plan for unmet sensory needs
His medication for a PRN anxiolytic
His ABC charts for the function of the behaviour
test.why: Constipation is common and can be life-threatening in people with a learning disability; a physical cause must be checked first.

whyNot.1: Sensory needs may matter, but physical pain is checked first.
whyNot.3: Functional assessment comes after physical causes are excluded.

explain.body: Use SBAR and lead with the change from baseline. Interpret NEWS2 against the person's usual state. Carer concern is a trigger to act. Escalate again if not satisfied.

test.q: When escalating concern about a non-verbal patient with a learning disability, what should the nurse emphasise first?
options: That the patient has a learning disability
How the patient differs from their usual baseline
That the family are anxious and want answers
That staffing makes close observation difficult
test.why: Leading with the change from baseline makes the clinical significance clear and counters overshadowing.

whyNot.0: The diagnosis alone can invite overshadowing; the change is what matters.
whyNot.2: Family concern is relevant, but the clinical change should lead.
whyNot.3: Staffing is a separate issue from the clinical concern.
